The announcements this week by England’s Environment Agency and Natural Resources Wales mark the third such event over the past five years, and come in the wake of four record-breaking heatwaves since May which have fuelled huge wildfires and left farmers, wildlife and protected habitats running out of water.

item.title: How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia
item.description:
How Israeli presence in Forest City exposes the Zionist-aligned underbelly of Malaysia

Submitted by Miriyam Ilavenil on Fri, 07/31/2026 - 09:12
The controversy has fuelled debate over the country's pro-Palestine policy and broader questions about Zionist control
People hold placards and Palestinian flags during a demonstration marking Al-Quds (Jerusalem) Day after Friday prayers in Kuala Lumpur, 13 March 2026 (Mohd Rasfan/AFP)
Off

On 15 July, Anwar Ibrahim, the prime minister of Malaysia, said authorities would deport any Israeli nationals found in the Southeast Asian country, while strongly expressing that Malaysia would "not compromise" on its immigration policies.

"If we find any Israeli, we will deport them immediately because we do not recognise Israel," the prime minister said, according to local media reports.

His comments came as officials investigated allegations that Israelis were involved in a private residential and technology community in the southern state of Johor.

Johor Chief Minister Dato Onn Hafiz Ghazi stated that at the state level, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) and relevant agencies would re-examine the Network School's business regulations. 

He also called on the federal bodies of the Home Affairs, Immigration Department, Police and Customs Department to investigate the allegations of Israelis in the Network School. Malaysia's federal Home Affairs Ministry later that day ordered a probe.

After two rounds of investigations, the Immigration Department said there were no violations among the 379 foreign nationals it investigated at the Network School, adding that 19 individuals' movements could not be traced.

The Immigration Department's Director-General Dato Zakaria Shaaban said that these individuals could have entered or left the country illegally. He added that authorities are on the lookout for the untraced individuals.

Then, on 17 July, Ghazi issued several notices to the Network School after authorities found that one of the premises linked to the school was operating without a valid business licence.  

On 23 July, the United States summoned Malaysia's ambassador to the US, Tan Sri Muhammad Shahrul Ikram Yaakob, to explain the nation's position on Israel. The Malaysian government stated that it would not change its immigration stance towards Israel. 

Founder of the Network School, Balaji Srinivasan, announced on X that he wanted an audience with the prime minister to restore his confidence in Malaysia as an investable jurisdiction. 

Balaji Srinivasan: Venture capitalist and Zionist ally

Balaji Srinivasan, a former Silicon Valley venture capitalist and Stanford professor, publicised the Network State in 2022. 

Marketing it vaguely as a startup society focused on peace, Srinivasan proposed building a "startup country" from the internet up. 

The Network State describes the idea on its website as "crowdfunding territory" and "eventually gaining diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states".

Malaysia vows to deport Israelis found in digital nomads community
Read More »

The website calls this new state a composition of an "ethnic diaspora" in which emigrants are connected with "the motherland" and come together in person to build dwellings and structures.

"In a sense, you can think of each physical outpost of this digital community as a cloud embassy," it says, adding that "recruits can visit either the virtual or physical parts of a network state, beta test it, and decide to leave or stay".

Along with Srinivasan, the Network State is financed by tech entrepreneurs Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Joe Lonsdale, Patri Friedman, as well as crypto firms like Coinbase and Praxis.

Peter Thiel's Palantir has invested in Israeli military and surveillance startups accused of providing technological support to Israeli intelligence in the Palestinian genocide.

Praxis, a company funded by Marc Andreessen, Sam Altman and Peter Thiel, has proposed building a tech-owned city on Greenland after US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to take the territory by force. Trump has also shared the intent to build a Trump luxury resort in Gaza.

Critics argue that the Network State model resembles historical settler projects because it envisions digitally organised communities purchasing or controlling physical land.

Some scholars have also pointed to Srinivasan's frequent references to Israel as an example of successful nation-building, arguing that his writings draw inspiration from Israel's state-building experience.

In 2024, centring the pitch around proximity to Singapore, Srinivasan formed the Network School in Malaysia's Forest City, in the southern state of Johor.

Making of Forest City: Fisherfolk and reclaimed land 

The project's location in Malaysia's Forest City in Johor has added another layer of complexity. In a recent video podcast, Srinivasan alludes to the Network School being born out of "nothing into something". 

The "nothing" on which the multibillion-dollar development is built is termed "reclaimed" land in Johor and has faced criticism for its environmental impact on coastal ecosystems and local fishing communities.

Forest City is a joint venture between China's Country Garden Group and Malaysian private company Iskandar Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd (EDBS), whose shareholders include Johor's Sultan Ibrahim and interests linked to the ruling political party, United Malays National Organisation.

Read More »

Between July 2024 and June 2025, Malaysia attracted about $759m in data centre investments, with Johor emerging as a key hub alongside the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone. 

An extensive investigation by Mongabay revealed how a Chinese builder began construction in the Forest City without an environmental impact assessment, devastating local seagrass and sparking strong community criticism.

The project also saw massive sand dumping, which destroyed marine habitats and hundreds of hectares of traditional fishing grounds. 

Rights groups have previously raised concerns that most of Forest City's workforce comprised low-wage labourers from South Asia, especially Bangladesh. 

The project has drawn controversy again, after allegations circulated online that Israeli nationals were participating in the Network School. 

The dispute exposed contradictions between Malaysia's pro-Palestine foreign policy and its efforts to attract international technology investment, even as government officials have maintained that enforcement actions were based on regulatory compliance rather than political considerations.

Neocolonial Malaysia: US imperial base, pro-Zionist hub 

The developments surrounding the Network School have fuelled a wider debate over Malaysia's balancing of its support for the Palestinian cause and economic relationship with the United States and western capitals.

The country is shaped by a constitutional monarchy, where political and economic power is concentrated among the federal government, state authorities and royal institutions.

Israel condemns Malaysia's decision to bar its athletes from competing
Read More »

The Federation of Malaysia was violently formed in 1963 and has since come down heavily on the people's movement in Malaya (West Malaysia) and Borneo (East Malaysia), allowing projects like the Network State to be built without much public resistance.

In 2024, Malaysia allowed a subsidiary of BlackRock to join a consortium to take ownership of Malaysia Airports (MAHB), Khazanah Nasional and the Employees Provident Fund (EPF), under the jurisdiction of the finance ministry led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

Civil society organisations in the country called on Ibrahim to make "the right and conscionable decision" by excluding the "Zionist entity conducting a settler-colonial and racist genocide in Gaza". 

Local media reported that the administration "launched an aggressive media campaign to discredit critics of the plan". 

In April, several international defence companies with business relationships with the Israeli military participated in the Defence Services Asia (DSA) and National Security (Natsec) Asia 2026 exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.

Companies included Lockheed Martin, a US defence contractor that supplies aircraft and other military equipment to Israel, MBDA, a European missile manufacturer whose products have been exported to Israel, and Colt's Manufacturing, a US firearms producer whose weapons are used by the Israeli military. 

Malaysia police free Palestinian kidnapped by Mossad agents: Report
Read More »

Civil society members pointed to investment links between Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby and Caterpillar, whose bulldozers have been used by the Israeli military in demolitions in the occupied Palestinian territories.

They also cited the operations of Australian rare earths producer Lynas in Malaysia, arguing that rare earth minerals are used in global defence supply chains, including those serving Israel.

Malaysian ports have also been used to facilitate shipments linked to Israel's military supply chain during the ongoing genocide in Gaza, transporting $885 million in weapons to Israel between 2023 and 2025, Al Jazeera investigations have found. 

In 2025, Ibrahim welcomed Trump during the ASEAN Summit despite protests against his visit.

Police maintained tight security, while rights groups accused Malaysian authorities of detaining and intimidating pro-Palestine protesters during peaceful demonstrations.

While officials have maintained that the country cannot sever ties with every international company that has business links to Israel, the Network School controversy has exposed Malaysia's projection of a pro-Palestine foreign policy alongside its ambition to attract foreign technology investment.

Johor remains a key destination for data centres and AI investments as part of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone.

Why remittance inflows stay below $3b for second straight month
item.description:
Remittance inflows declined again in July after falling in June, with expatriate Bangladeshis sending home nearly $2.86 billion during the month.

In June, remittances totalled $2.82 billion, according to data released on Sunday by Bangladesh Bank. The decline comes after six consecutive months in which monthly remittance inflows exceeded $3 billion.

The drop has raised concerns among many bankers, who note that remittances are one of Bangladesh’s largest sources of foreign currency.

item.title: Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest
item.description:
A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan’s northwestern Swat Valley
Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state’s inability to protect citizens.
Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence
The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012.
Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators.
“The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station,” a local police official said
No group has claimed responsibility for the crime.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack.
“Terrorists,” said Zardari, “will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state.”
Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces.
The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan’s military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area.
The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active.
The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries.
Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network.

item.title: Cabinet scraps essential drugs list and pricing method
item.description:
The Cabinet has approved a proposal to scrap the Essential Drugs List 2026 and the Drug Price Determination Method 2026.

The proposal was approved on Monday afternoon during a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.

A press release issued by the Cabinet Division following the meeting confirmed the decision.

According to the press release, the government remains committed to ensuring safe, effective, high-quality, and affordable medicines for the public.

It further said that the rationale behind scrapping the Essential Drugs List 2026 and the Drug Price Determination Method 2026 stems from a statutory requirement under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 2023, which stipulates that the National Drug Advisory Council must be consulted prior to formulating the essential drugs list—a procedure that was not observed.

Formulated in January 2026 during the interim government’s tenure, the essential drugs list and pricing policy were drafted without consulting the National Drug Advisory Council.

A writ petition challenging their legal validity was subsequently filed in the High Court, where the matter currently remains sub judice.

Meanwhile, on 29 June, the National Drug Advisory Council was constituted in accordance with the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 2023. The Cabinet has also approved a proposal to include the Director General of health services in this advisory council.

However, despite the cancellation of this year’s essential drugs list and pricing policy, the essential drugs list formulated under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s 1994 order, along with the government pricing mechanism for those medicines, will remain in force as before.

A decision has been taken to update the essential drugs list. Drug prices will be determined in a manner that avoids placing an additional burden on the people while maintaining healthy competition in the market.

Zakir Hossain, former Secretary General of the Bangladesh Association of Pharmaceutical Industries (BAPI), welcomed the Cabinet’s decision.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said, “The pharmaceutical industry had been facing a stagnant situation for nearly two years. The Cabinet’s decision will resolve this impasse and restore stability to the market. Industry owners have shown complete sincerity, and it is hoped that the prevailing legal complexities will now be resolved.”

These include the entry into Gaza of the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the deployment of an International Stabilization Force (ISF), and the start of desperately needed reconstruction.

Most crucially, the emphasis on disarmament has precluded any discussion of Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza. Instead, Israeli control of the territory has increased significantly since the start of the ceasefire, from about 53 per cent of Gaza in October (delineated by the so-called ‘Yellow Line’) to nearly 70 per cent today.

President Trump’s recent announcement that Hamas has agreed to his disarmament plan may change that dynamic. By essentially calling Israel’s bluff, Hamas’s move could potentially put external pressure on Israel in Gaza for the first time in months. The question is whether the Board of Peace in general, and Trump in particular, are willing to put the necessary pressure on both parties to move past the current stalemate.

Swift change unlikely

In reality, it is unlikely that a timeline for decommissioning weapons or drawing down troops will be agreed anytime soon.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will likely seek to drag out any further negotiations as much as possible; the last thing he wants as he goes into October’s elections is US pressure to withdraw from Gaza. Any public suggestion from Netanyahu that Israel would reduce its control in Gaza or make concessions to Hamas would likely lose him his voter base. (Far from accepting Israel’s withdrawal from the enclave, right-wing Israeli ministers have already announced plans for new settlements in Gaza.)

Dragging out the process also suits Hamas. Agreeing to Trump’s plan is likely a pragmatic move by new Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya. It keeps the group in the conversation about Gaza’s future and may improve its position in relation to the Board of Peace – potentially even shifting the onus of intransigence to Israel. But Hamas knows that the actual decommissioning of its weapons will not be immediate.

Indeed, both actors will likely double down on sequencing demands that have stymied previous attempts to reach agreements in Gaza: Israel will likely require full Hamas disarmament before withdrawal, while Hamas will likely insist on Israeli withdrawal before decommissioning weapons.

Already, Israeli officials have said they will not pull back without ‘genuine disarmament’ by Hamas and have expressed ‘serious security concerns’ about the deal to the White House.

Israel reportedly insisted to the Board of Peace that it reserved the right to strike areas set to be handed over to the ISF and objected to Qatar and Turkey (both central mediators in the agreement with Hamas) being involved in the roadmap’s future verification stages. It also reportedly demanded that Hamas’s weapons be destroyed rather than stored after confiscation.

Hamas is also hedging. It has stated that its moves will be contingent on Israel ending ‘all forms of aggression’, as well as withdrawing to the October ceasefire’s ‘Yellow Line,’ facilitating the entry of the ISF and NCAG, and meeting humanitarian aid obligations.

Hamas has also rejected Israeli demands that weapons be destroyed, and has intentionally avoided the language of disarmament or surrender. Indeed, the term ‘disarmament’ does not appear anywhere in Trump’s roadmap, relying instead on ‘decommissioning,’ modelled in part on Northern Ireland’s process.

Furthermore, Hamas will likely resist full decommissioning without a broader negotiated process to realize a Palestinian state. The disarmament plan does not mention Palestinian self-determination directly, but it does refer (in Article 8) to the completion of the ‘remaining commitments under [the] Sharm [el] Sheikh Protocol,’ Trump’s initial 20-point plan for Gaza. Point 19 of that plan refers to a ‘credible pathway for Palestinian self-determination and statehood.’ Netanyahu has fully rejected the notion of Palestinian statehood, while Hamas will insist upon it.

US and Board of Peace officials have stressed the ‘zero trust’ nature of the roadmap, emphasizing that it will proceed based solely on externally verified steps and conditions. But even reciprocal processes require one side to take the first step. It is more likely that both sides will buy time by telling the Board of Peace at least some semblance of what it wants to hear. Meanwhile, they will both likely avoid any real commitments by objecting to any one of the myriad thorny details required to actually implement a plan.

External pressure

In this context, external commitment and pressure are crucial. For Hamas, the mediating efforts of Egypt, Turkey, and Qatar have been essential in getting the group to publicly accept the agreement. But these regional states will have less leverage in getting Hamas to implement it, as they are not physically on the ground in Gaza to enforce commitments or to provide security guarantees.

On the Israeli side, it remains unclear the extent to which the US – and by extension, the Board of Peace – will be willing to impose substantive pressure on Israel to even discuss withdrawal.

There are several factors to consider here. First is the question of Trump’s personal commitment to shepherding the agreement beyond the fanfare of the initial headlines. If the past year is any guide, the disarmament roadmap could easily become yet another casualty of Trump’s slapdash approach to diplomacy, in which a numbered plan is released with bravado, but then flounders without the long, arduous subsequent work required to make it operational.

item.title: PCB appoints South Africa's Michael Smith as batting coach for Pakistan men's cricket team
item.description:
Former South African cricketer Michael Smith has been appointed as the batting coach of the Pakistan men’s cricket team for two years, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) announced on Tuesday.

According to a press release issued by the PCB, the “46-year-old will work with the team across both red-ball and white-ball formats”.

He will join the Pakistan team ahead of the three-match Test series against England, commencing on Aug 19, the press release stated.

Elaborating on Smith’s experience, the press release stated that he had featured in 89 first-class matches, 72 List-A matches and 16 T20 matches between 2003 and 2013.

“The right-handed batter scored 7,029 runs across the three formats, including nine centuries and 40 half-centuries,” the PCB said.

Smith, who holds a Level 4 coaching qualification, has served on the coaching staffs of three HBL Pakistan Super League (PSL) franchises — Islamabad United, Karachi Kings and Multan Sultans, it added

The press release further stated that he has also worked as a batting coach with Australian franchise Hobart Hurricanes and Cricket Tasmani.

As a coaching consultant, Smith has worked with South Africa’s KZN Inland and Eastern Province, the press release added.

Prior to Smith’s appointment, former Test batter Asad Shafiq was appointed as Pakistan’s interim batting coach in April 2026 for the Bangladesh Test series. Shafiq is currently also accompanying the Pakistan team for its two-match Test series in the West Indies.

Before Shafiq’s interim appointment, Shahid Aslam had been serving as Pakistan’s batting coach since replacing former Test captain Mohammad Yousuf in the role in November 2024.

item.title: Bangladesh asks India to clarify stance on ousted PM Hasina's planned speech in New Delhi
item.description:
Bangladesh has asked India to clarify its stance on exiled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s planned virtual address from New Delhi, warning that allowing political activities by a fugitive could hurt improving bilateral relations.

The remarks were Bangladesh’s first official response to Hasina’s planned appearance at an August 5 event hosted by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in New Delhi, marking the second anniversary of the student-led uprising that toppled her government.

The issue comes as Dhaka continues to seek Hasina’s extradition from India, where she has lived since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024.

Despite multiple cases against her, Hasina told Reuters in an interview that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December.

“We are moving forward with India with a forward-looking approach. We don’t want that progress to be affected,” Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told reporters late on Monday.

“India has to be clear about its stance.”

The FCCSA said Hasina, 78, will address the New Delhi event by video link alongside her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, and other speakers. The club did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Bangladesh government concerns.

Islam said Bangladesh had repeatedly conveyed its concerns to India over Hasina and other Awami League leaders making political statements from Indian soil.

“We do not want India-Bangladesh relations to be harmed by statements from fugitive accused individuals,” she said, adding that India had previously indicated it did not expect fugitives to engage in political activities from its territory.

While stressing that the event was not organised by the Indian government, Islam said Dhaka would raise the matter through diplomatic channels if necessary.

There was no immediate response from the Indian foreign ministry.

Relations between the neighbours have been strained since Hasina’s removal from power, although both sides have recently signalled a willingness to rebuild ties through greater engagement and cooperation since Tarique Rahman’s government took office after February’s election.

Hasina has remained in India since her government was overthrown after weeks of deadly protests. Bangladesh has since sought her extradition, and in 2025 she was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown, which the United Nations estimated killed up to 1,400 people. Hasina has rejected the verdict as legally void.

item.title: Trapped by war, Bangladesh seafarer recounts Gulf ordeal

"I tried to stay calm because I was responsible for 31 lives, a ship worth $40 million, and cargo valued at $8.2 million," the 51-year-old Bangladeshi mariner told AFP, back home after the ordeal.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank removes loan limits on Sonali Bank, allowing lending flexibility
item.description:
The Bangladesh Bank has withdrawn the lending limits previously imposed on five major branches of the state-owned Sonali Bank. As a result, the bank will now be able to extend loans without branch-specific lending caps, subject to customer applications and applicable regulations.

Sonali Bank had informed the central bank that retaining the lending restrictions would adversely affect the economy, prompting the Bangladesh Bank to take this decision.

The lending limits had long applied to Sonali Bank's office branch, Foreign Exchange Corporate Branch, Shilpa Bhaban Corporate Branch, Shaheed Abrar Fahad Avenue Corporate Branch, and Laldighi Corporate Branch in Chattogram.

Depending on the branch, customers could previously obtain loans of no more than Tk 50 million (5 crore) to Tk 200 million (20 crore). With the withdrawal of these limits, no branch of Sonali Bank will now face restrictions on the amount of loans it can sanction.

The Bangladesh Bank first imposed lending limits on Sonali Bank in 2007 under the state-owned bank reform programme financed by the World Bank.

It further strengthened its oversight of the bank following the Hall-Mark financial scandal in 2012. These measures gradually helped strengthen the bank's financial position.

More recently, Sonali Bank sought the removal of the lending caps following pressure from influential clients, and the Bangladesh Bank responded positively.

However, the central bank has advised the bank to conduct thorough due diligence before approving new loans and to avoid extending credit to previously controversial or accused borrowers.

When contacted, Sonali Bank Managing Director Shawkat Ali Khan told Prothom Alo by telephone on Sunday, "Our five branches were subject to lending limits. Most of our good customers are attached to these branches. We were unable to provide loans even when they applied. Therefore, we requested the Bangladesh Bank to withdraw the lending restrictions. The central bank responded positively. We can now provide financing to our good customers."

How the lending caps were withdrawn

The local office branches of state-owned banks generally account for a substantial share of their total lending. In many cases, between 30 and 40 per cent of a bank's total loan portfolio is concentrated in a single branch.

Business clients typically prefer branches associated with the head office or other key corporate branches because they offer easier access and communication.

For this reason, the Bangladesh Bank originally imposed lending limits on these five branches. Of Sonali Bank's total loan portfolio, around 27 per cent is concentrated in its Local Office Branch.

Among the state-owned banks, Sonali Bank is currently in the strongest financial position. The bank recorded a profit of Tk 9.88 billion (988 crore) in 2024, which increased to Tk 13.13 billion (1313 crore) by the end of 2025. Based on profit, Sonali Bank ranked as the country's third most profitable bank among both public and private sector banks at the end of last year.

Consequently, the central bank capped working capital loans at Tk 50 million (5 crore) per customer at that branch and Tk 200 million (20 crore) per customer at each of the other four branches.

Following Sonali Bank's application, the Bangladesh Bank increased the lending limit for the Local Office Branch from Tk 50 million to Tk 200 million on 4 June.

However, it advised the bank to confine these loans to existing customers as well as cottage, micro, small and medium enterprises (CMSMEs), export-oriented industries, agricultural processing, import-substitution industries, pharmaceutical manufacturing, renewable energy, production and employment-generating sectors.

In a letter sent to the Bangladesh Bank on 14 July, Managing Director Shawkat Ali Khan stated that customers seeking quick and convenient access to credit were approaching those five branches.

However, the existing lending restrictions prevented the bank from meeting customer demand. He also noted that increasing credit flow to the private sector was essential for supporting overall economic growth and requested the removal of the lending caps.

At the end of last month, the Bangladesh Bank formally withdrew the restrictions and notified Sonali Bank of its decision.

Sonali Bank, Managing Director Shawkat Ali Khan Our five branches were subject to lending limits. Most of our good customers are attached to these branches. We were unable to provide loans even when they applied.

Approved loan facilities

Although the lending limit for Sonali Bank's Local Office Branch was Tk 200 million (20 crore), the bank approved a Tk 400 million (40 crore) loan for a company named Arham Multi Trading in May.

Records show that Rashedul Hasan, the proprietor of Arham Multi Trading, is the president of the Narsingdi Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

During the same period, Sonali Bank's Board of Directors approved a Tk 500 million (50 crore) loan for Munnu Fabrics, a company under the Munnu Group, which is also a client of the Local Office Branch.

The board approved the loan at its meeting on 13 May. At the same meeting, it also accepted the resignation of Afroza Khanam as managing director of Munnu Fabrics. She currently serves as the Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism.

Sonali Bank subsequently submitted the documents relating to both loan approvals to the Bangladesh Bank and sought special no-objection clearance.

At the same time, it requested the withdrawal of the branch lending limits. However, the central bank removed the lending restrictions, meaning these loans will no longer require Bangladesh Bank's approval before disbursement.

Sonali Bank Managing Director Shawkat Ali Khan also said, "The loan for the Monno Group had been approved once before. However, due to the circumstances at the time, the group did not receive the facility. The Board has now approved its disbursement. In addition, Arham Multi Trading is a good company. Since the lending limit has been withdrawn, the company will now receive the loan in accordance with the regulations."

Sonali Bank's financial position

Among the state-owned banks, Sonali Bank is currently in the strongest financial position. The bank recorded a profit of Tk 9.88 billion (988 crore) in 2024, which increased to Tk 13.13 billion (1313 crore) by the end of 2025.

Based on profit, Sonali Bank ranked as the country's third most profitable bank among both public and private sector banks at the end of last year.

According to its financial statements, a significant portion of the bank's profit came from investments in government bills and bonds.

The bank currently has neither a capital shortfall nor any deficit in its statutory reserves. Compared with other state-owned banks, it has also maintained stronger management of non-performing loan risks.

According to Sonali Bank, its total deposits rose to Tk1.79879 trillion (179879 crore) in 2025, while its outstanding loan portfolio increased to Tk 1.04723 trillion (104723 crore).

Although the banking sector's overall non-performing loan ratio has exceeded 35 per cent, Sonali Bank's non-performing loan ratio remains at 18 per cent.

The bank's list of major defaulters includes the Hall-Mark Group, Beximco Group, Thermax Group, and Orion Group, among several others. As a result, the volume of non-performing loans has not declined. Nevertheless, Sonali Bank's loan-to-deposit ratio remains at approximately 58 per cent.

item.title: Lebanon and Israel hold new round of direct talks in Rome
item.description:
Lebanon and Israel held a fresh round of US-sponsored talks in Rome on Tuesday, with Beirut seeking Israel’s phased withdrawal from the country’s south.
Convoys carrying delegations from the two countries arrived in the morning to the US embassy in the Italian capital, where discussions are scheduled to run until Thursday.
At negotiations in Washington in June, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a framework deal that involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as “pilot zones.”
This week’s negotiations are the seventh round of Washington-mediated talks since Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel in support of its backer Iran.
Israel responded with heavy airstrikes and a ground invasion that Lebanon says have killed more than 4,300 people.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said on Tuesday that the direct negotiations would bring “nothing but shame, humiliation, and successive compromises” for Lebanon.
In a televised address, he also criticized Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun, saying he “has not acted as an arbiter, nor as a unifying figure, but has become biased and divisive, which is incompatible with his role and with Lebanon’s strength.”
On Monday, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani urged Lebanon and Israel to “continue in a constructive spirit, identifying shared solutions that will allow for the full implementation of the framework agreement,” his ministry said.
After talks last month, Israel’s military withdrew from the outskirts of the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiya, one of the first pilot zones.
The Lebanese army deployed to the area and has allowed residents to inspect their homes and businesses.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told a cabinet meeting on Monday that his country was pursuing “efforts towards successive Israeli withdrawals from Lebanese territory, leading to a full withdrawal.”
A US State Department official had told AFP that this week’s discussions would “include expanding the pilot zone process, resolving all outstanding border issues, and working on a comprehensive peace and security agreement.”
On Monday, US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa warned that “moving too quickly risks jeopardizing the very civilians this process is meant to protect.”
“It is better to take the time needed to get this right the first time. Doing so will allow subsequent pilot zones to move forward more efficiently,” Issa said.
“Both sides must agree on a clear, workable process before proceeding.”
The Lebanese army’s deployment is a major test, with experts expressing doubt over the authorities’ ability to disarm Hezbollah -- which opposes the Israel deal and refuses to surrender its weapons -- and prevent further non-state military activity.
Observers say Israel’s commitment to withdraw will also be tested when pilot zones are selected in areas fully under its occupation.
Violence in Lebanon has decreased since the Lebanon-Israel deal and the signing in June of a preliminary US-Iran agreement on the Middle East conflict.
But Lebanon continues to report intermittent Israeli strikes and shelling, as well as detonations and demolitions in southern villages.
